Dear Sir or Madam,

(1)    On 30 October 2025, the European Commission received notification of a
        proposed concentration pursuant to Article 4 of the Merger Regulation by which
       Vandemoortele NV (“Vandemoortele”, Belgium)  will  acquire  within  the
       meaning of Article 3(1)(b) of the Merger Regulation sole control of Délifrance
        S.A.   (“Délifrance”,  France)  by  way   of  purchase   of   shares   (the

1.    THE PARTIES
(2)     Vandemoortele is a food business founded in 1899 and headquartered in Ghent,
        Belgium. The company is a global manufacturer and supplier of frozen bakery
        products and plant-based food solutions such as fats, sauces, margarines and oils.
       Vandemoortele is mainly active in the production and supply of frozen bakery
        products on a business-to-business basis to both retail and foodservice customers
        across the EEA. (4)
(3)     Vandemoortele operates 36 production sites in total, 35 of which are located in
       Europe and one in the US. Five of Vandemoortele’s production sites are dedicated
         to the production of margarines, culinary oils and fats alone, while all the
        remaining sites are wholly or partially dedicated to the production of frozen
        bakery products, with a combined nominal production capacity of […] kilotonnes
        (“kT”). Most of the sites within the latter category are dedicated to the production
         of frozen bread and frozen morning goods, with fewer sites focusing on the
        production of frozen patisserie and frozen savoury snacks. (5)
(4)     Délifrance is a global manufacturer and supplier of frozen bakery products and
         of certain consumer packaged products, founded in 1978 and headquartered in
         Ivry-sur-Seine, France. The company sells frozen bakery products on a business-
         to-business basis to both retail and foodservice customers across the EEA, mainly
         in the United Kingdom, France and Italy. (6) Délifrance is part of the Vivescia
        Group, a cooperative owned by 7,500 cooperative farmers. Its ultimate parent
       company is S.C.A Vivescia, Société Coopérative Agricole. (7)
(5)      Délifrance operates 14 production sites, 12 of which are situated in Europe and 2
         in the Asia Pacific Region. Délifrance’s total annual production capacity is […]
        kT, of which […] kT is in the Asia Pacific Region. (8)

2.    THE CONCENTRATION
(6)    On 12 June 2025, the Parties entered into a share purchase agreement whereby
       Vandemoortele will acquire 100% of the share capital and voting rights of
         Délifrance, therefore acquiring sole control within the meaning of Article 3(1)(b)
         of the Merger Regulation.

(18)    According to the Notifying Party, the Transaction allows Vandemoortele to
       expand its activities in Europe and the US (where the company already owns a

         get access  to Délifrance’s production  sites and  distribution networks, and
        strengthen the retail and food service channels. The Transaction also enables
       Vandemoortele to expand its product offerings with Délifrance’s frozen bakery
         products, which customers reportedly consider as being of high quality. (20)

4.4.2.   Product market
(21)    In this Section, the Commission will first analyse the market for the manufacture
       and supply of frozen bakery products (with possible segmentations within this
        market) (Section 4.4.2.1) and then analyse the segmentation per sales channels
         for frozen bakery products (Section 4.4.2.2).

4.4.2.1. Manufacture and supply of frozen bakery products
(22)    The Commission will first assess the market for frozen bakery products in general
          (in this Section 4.4.2.1.1) and then examine further segmentations in relation to
        frozen morning goods (Section 4.4.2.1.2) and frozen bread (Section 4.4.2.1.3)
         specifically.

4.4.2.1.1.     Manufacture and supply of frozen bakery products in general

4.4.2.1.1.1.   Commission past practice
(23)    In prior decisions, the Commission considered that the market for the manufacture
       and supply of frozen bakery products was a separate market from the manufacture
       and supply of other frozen foods (21). The Commission further considered
        segmenting said market per category of products namely (i) frozen bread, (ii)
        frozen morning goods, (iii) frozen pastries and cakes (22), and (iv) frozen savoury
        snacks (23) ultimately leaving the exact market definition open.

4.4.2.1.1.2.   The Notifying Party’s view
(24)    The Notifying Party does not dispute the fact that the market for frozen bakery
        products can be further segmented based on the category of products into: (i)
        frozen bread, (ii) frozen morning goods, (iii) frozen patisserie, and (iv) frozen
        savoury snacks, in line with the Commission’s past decisional practice. (24)
(25)    The Notifying Party submits that no further segmentation of the four main
         categories of frozen bakery products is warranted, arguing that products within
        each  category  are  substitutable  both  from  a  demand-  and  supply-side
         perspective. (25)
(26)     Specifically, on the demand-side, the Notifying Party argues that consumers
        consider the products within each of the four main categories as interchangeable
       and would likely switch between different products in case of a price increase. (26)
(27)   On the supply-side, the Notifying Party argues that suppliers can reposition their
        production lines and adjust product mixes easily and at low cost to produce
         different products within each of the four main categories of frozen bakery

4.4.2.1.2.     Manufacture and supply of frozen morning goods

4.4.2.1.2.1.   Commission past practice

4.4.2.1.2.2.   The Notifying Party’s view

(31)    The Notifying Party also submits that no further segmentation of laminated dough

(32)    In addition, the Notifying Party submits that “sweet treats”  / donuts do not

(34)    Given these indications, the Commission assessed whether the smaller product
         categories within frozen morning goods constitute separate relevant product
        markets by examining the scope for potential demand-side and supply-side
         substitution in line with the Market Definition Notice. (35)

4.4.2.1.2.3.1. Demand-side substitutability
(35)   As explained in the Market Definition Notice, the main approach used by the
       Commission to define the relevant product market  is that of assessing the
          substitutability of products from the perspective of the customer (demand
         substitution). Situations of sufficiently strong demand substitution arise when
        customers would switch easily from the products of the undertaking(s) involved
         to readily available alternative products. The Commission includes those products
         in the same relevant product market as they constitute effective and immediate
        competitive constraints. (36) Factors that the Commission would consider include
        customer preferences relating to product characteristics, prices, functionalities,
        intended use, barriers to switching and switching costs. (37)
(36)    In relation to a distinction between: (i) laminated dough products (e.g. croissant,
       Danish pastries) (38); (ii) risen dough products (e.g. brioche); and (iii) fried dough
        products (e.g. donuts), the Commission’s investigation indicates that these may
        each form separate product markets.
(37)     First, customers explained that they generally purchase frozen morning goods at
         the level of the individual product, suggesting that each caters for a specific need.
        For example, a market participant responded that “The procurement process
         usually takes place in annual tender format where each specific product is
        tendered separately within each core category.” (39) A customer further indicated
         that “supply contracts and negotiations take place either for one specific product
       each time, which is the most common, or for more than one product / groups of
        products, [which happens] more rarely”. (40)
(38)    This also suggests that within laminated dough products, each product (such as
         croissants, pains au chocolat, Danish  pastries  etc.) might not be seen as
         substitutable from a demand-side perspective. However, as explained further
        below, laminated dough products appear to be substitutable from a supply-side
         perspective.

(40)     Third, in relation to laminated dough products specifically, the majority of
        customers who participated in the market investigation responded that they would
         either not replace laminated dough products with other types of frozen morning
        goods, or that they would only do so under exceptional circumstances. (42)
(41)    For example,

        •     In terms of product characteristics, customers referred to differences in
                quality, taste and freshness, which made laminated dough products not
             comparable with other products within frozen morning goods. (43)

        •    Laminated dough products also differ in their applications and customer
               expectations. As one customer noted: “My company would never replace
            Laminated Dough with other Frozen Morning Goods because Laminated
            dough products represent a very specific product related to a particular
            moment'  consumption  that  cannot  be  replaced  with  other  similar
              products”, (44) while according to another customer: “Les indispensables de
                la viennoiserie sont les produits à base de pâte feuilletée type croissant, pain
            au chocolat etc. Il n'est pas possible de remplacer ces produits par des
                substituts notamment au regard des préférences de consommation des
            consommateurs français.” (45)
(42)    This  lack  of  demand-side  substitutability was  further  confirmed by  the
        competitors of the Parties in the market investigation, with the majority indicating
        they would not offer their customers other frozen morning goods as a replacement
         for laminated dough products. (46) Market participants referred to differences in
        customer  needs,  product  characteristics and  price  points  to  support  this
        conclusion. For example, one competitor noted: “Customer needs are different.
        Can’t be replaced by different products (e.g. if customer wants croissant, he buys
         croissants)”. (47)
(43)    Based on the above considerations, in particular differences in the procurement
         of the products, product characteristics, customer needs and prices, the three
        product categories listed above in paragraph (33) are not substitutable from a
        demand-side perspective.

        products that are not substitutes for customers, and where this leads to similar
        conditions of competition across the range of such related products. In such cases,
             it may be appropriate to include such related products in the relevant product
        market, provided the constraining effect of supply substitution across the range of
        products is equivalent to that of demand substitution in terms of effectiveness and
        immediacy. (48) Supply-side substitution may be found where suppliers are able
         to switch production between products in the range of related products (with only
         insignificant additional sunk costs or risks when they switch production). (49)
(45)    In the present case, various elements suggest that a segmentation based on the
        product categories referred to in paragraph (33) above is appropriate also from the
        supply-side perspective.
(46)     First, switching production between laminated dough products (e.g. croissant,
       Danish pastries); risen dough products (e.g. brioche); and fried dough products
          (e.g. donuts) appears difficult. The majority of competitors indicated that their
        production lines were not able to produce all three categories of frozen morning
        goods. (50) This is because specialised equipment is required for each product
         category. Indeed, one competitor detailed that “the kind of process of a croissant,
       a doughnut or a brioche is completely different. Therefore, you cannot use the
       same kind of equipment”. Another competitor explained in more details that: “The
        production technology for laminated dough products can cover the following
        product categories: French laminated dough products (French viennoiserie),
       Danish pastries. […] If the lamination step in the production line is skipped, risen
       dough / brioche products can be produced on the same line. This switch is not
         often made. The production process for fried dough products is significantly
         different (need for a frying step). The switch from laminated dough products to
         fried dough products is therefore never done.” (51). These difficulties in switching
        production are further supported by the initial market inquiry conducted during
         the pre-notification calls with competitors. (52)
(47)    The above also suggests that each individual product within the laminated dough
        product market (e.g. croissants, pains au chocolat, Danish pastries) can be
        produced with the same production technology, on the same line. In spite of a lack
         of demand-side substitutability between the laminated dough products at an
         individual level, this evidence supports defining a market for laminated dough as
        a whole.
(48)    Second,  the  Parties’ own manufacturing  operations  are  organised around
        production lines that are dedicated to a specific product category, such as

5.    COMPETITIVE ASSESSMENT

5.1.    Legal Framework
(88)    Pursuant to Articles 2(2) and 2(3) of the Merger Regulation, the Commission must
         assess whether a proposed concentration would significantly impede effective
        competition in the internal market or in a substantial part of  it, in particular
        through the creation or strengthening of a dominant position. In this respect, a
       merger can entail horizontal (non-coordinated and/or coordinated) and/or non-
         horizontal effects.
(89)    The Horizontal Merger Guidelines describe horizontal non-coordinated effects as
         follows: “A merger may significantly impede effective competition in a market by
       removing important  competitive  constraints on one or more  sellers, who
        consequently have increased market power. The most direct effect of the merger
         will be the loss of competition between the merging firms. For example, if prior
         to the merger one of the merging firms had raised its price, it would have lost
       some sales to the other merging firm. The merger removes this particular
         constraint. Non-merging firms in the same market can also benefit from the
        reduction of competitive pressure that results from the merger, since the merging
         firms' price increase may switch some demand to the rival firms, which, in turn,
      may find it profitable to increase their prices. The reduction in these competitive
         constraints could lead to significant price increases in the relevant market.
        Generally, a merger  giving  rise  to  such  non-coordinated  effects would
         significantly impede  effective competition by creating or strengthening the
       dominant  position  of a  single  firm, one which,  typically, would have an
        appreciably  larger  market  share  than  the  next  competitor  post-merger.
        Furthermore, mergers in oligopolistic markets involving the elimination of
        important competitive constraints that the merging parties previously exerted
       upon each other together with a reduction of competitive pressure on the
        remaining competitors may, even where there is little likelihood of coordination
        between the members of the oligopoly, also result in a significant impediment to
         competition. The Merger Regulation clarifies that all mergers giving rise to such
        non-coordinated effects shall also be declared incompatible with the common
        market.” (102)
(90)    The Horizontal Merger Guidelines list a number of factors which may influence
        whether or not significant horizontal non-coordinated effects are likely to result
       from a merger, such as the large market shares of the merging firms, the fact that
         the merging firms are close competitors, the limited possibilities for customers to
        switch suppliers, or the fact that the merger would eliminate an important
        competitive force. (103) Not all of these factors need to be present to make
         significant non-coordinated effects likely and it is not an exhaustive list. (104)
(91)     Finally, the Horizontal Merger Guidelines describe a number of factors, which
        could counteract the harmful effects of the merger on competition, including the

6.1.    Framework for the assessment of the commitments
(355)   Where a notified concentration raises serious doubts as to its compatibility with
         the internal market or the functioning of the EEA agreement, the parties may
       modify the notified concentration so as to remove the grounds for the serious
        doubts identified by the Commission with a view to having it declared compatible
        with the internal market pursuant to Article 6(1)(b) in conjunction with Article
        6(2) of the Merger Regulation.
(356)  As set out in the Commission Notice on Remedies, (351) commitments have to
         eliminate the Commission’s competition concerns entirely and they have to be
        comprehensive  and  effective from  all  points  of  view. (352)  In  Phase  I,
       commitments offered by the parties can only be accepted where the competition
       problem is readily identifiable and can easily be remedied. The competition
       problem therefore needs to be so straightforward and the remedies so clear-cut
         that  it  is not necessary to enter into an in-depth investigation and that the
       commitments are sufficient to clearly rule out serious doubts within the meaning
         of Article 6(1)(c) of the Merger Regulation. (353)
(357)   In assessing whether or not the commitments proposed by the parties would
         restore effective competition, the Commission considers all relevant factors,
        including the type, scale and scope of the proposed commitments judged by
         reference to the structure and particular characteristics of the market in which the
        competition concerns arise, including the position of the Parties and other players
       on the market. (354)
(358)   In order for the commitments to comply with those principles, they must be
        capable of being implemented effectively within a short period of time. (355) The
       Commission must determine with the requisite degree of certainty, at the time of
           its decision, that they will be fully implemented and that they are likely to
        maintain effective competition in the market. (356)
(359)  As regards the form of acceptable commitments, the Merger Regulation leaves
         discretion to the Commission as long as the commitments meet the requisite
         standards. Structural commitments, in particular  divestitures, will meet the
        conditions set out above only in so far as the Commission is able to conclude with
         the requisite degree of certainty, at the time of its Decision, that it will be possible
         to implement them and that it will be likely that the new commercial structures

               they fail to appoint the third expert within 15 working days from their appointment,

                 Parties and the Purchaser, and a suitably qualified and experienced expert.

       Monitoring Trustee. The language of the process shall be English.

               reasonably requires to consider the matters referred to them;
